nameStory: The "mother-of-many" part of this lichen's name comes from its remarkable ability to reproduce through tiny leaf-like structures called phyllidia that cover its surface like countless little offspring. These small, scale-like growths can break off and grow into new lichens, making the parent truly a "mother of many." The "pelt" part refers to its leather-like texture and the way it lies flat against surfaces like an animal hide.
description: Mother-of-many pelt is a large, leaf-like lichen that spreads across rocks and soil like a living leather mat. It's part of the pelt lichen family, which are known for their distinctive lobed, foliose (leafy) growth form. This particular species is covered with tiny, raised bumps called phyllidia that give it a uniquely textured appearance. It can grow quite large, sometimes reaching 6-8 inches across, making it one of the more substantial lichens you might encounter.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Covered with numerous small, leaf-like bumps (phyllidia) that feel rough and granular when you gently touch them - like running your finger over coarse sandpaper

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Large, spreading, leaf-like lobes that lie flat against the substrate with slightly raised, wavy edges

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish-gray on top when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet; underside is pale with distinct dark veins

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes can be 1-2 inches wide, with the entire lichen colony reaching 4-8 inches across

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Found on acidic soil, mossy rocks, and occasionally on tree bases in shaded, humid locations

habitat: This rare lichen prefers shaded, humid environments in New England's older forests, particularly on acidic soil and moss-covered rocks. Look for it in cool, north-facing slopes of mountains and in deep ravines where moisture lingers. It's associated with mature forest ecosystems and may be found near streams or in areas where fog and dew provide consistent moisture.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant and noticeable as spring moisture activates growth; the phyllidia may appear more pronounced as the lichen expands.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more contracted during dry periods, but maintains its characteristic bumpy texture throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its best in the cool, moist conditions of autumn when morning dews keep it hydrated and colorful.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow cover and can actually appear quite green during winter thaws when moisture is abundant.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a walking nursery - those bumpy phyllidia on its surface can detach and blow away in the wind, each one capable of starting an entirely new lichen colony miles away, making it one of nature's most efficient long-distance colonizers.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pelt lichens, but the dense covering of phyllidia (tiny leaf-like bumps) makes it unique - other pelt lichens might have smooth surfaces, soredia (powdery granules), or different reproductive structures, but none have this distinctive "bumpy leather" texture.
contextualKnowledge: With only 2 recorded observations in New England, this is considered an extremely rare lichen in our region. Finding one would be a significant discovery worth reporting to local naturalist groups or citizen science platforms like iNaturalist.
compareHints: Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface. While other pelt lichens might have soredia (powdery reproductive structures) or isidia (coral-like projections), this species is unique in having numerous small, leaf-like phyllidia scattered across its entire upper surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
